new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. the copy we hold contains the passage exactly as the report quotes it. I re-queried Open Library search-inside independently (raw response. overlapping highlights in, both in the mang1394 folder, appended). The phrase "Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable" returns exactly one hit in the whole IA full-text index: item linguisticanalys0000tuck = Tucker & Bryan 1966, Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa. Overlapping snippets reproduce the whole chain: "..MORU-MANGBETU LANGUAGES 31 / Falling and Rising tones are found only in MANGBETU-MEJE.. In all these languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mangbetu is a tone language (H, L plus falling/rising contours per Demolin 1991); on top of tone, Larochette (as reported by Tucker & Bryan) observed a tendency for stress to fall on the penultimate syllable of the word or phrase, sometimes accompanied by extra-high pitch. Hyman 1977 and Ruhlen 1975/76 (via Downing 2004: 111) accordingly list Mangbetu as 'dominant penultimate stress (as well as tone)'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported in the accessible passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Described only as a 'tendency'; no exceptions given in the snippet. The scanned example 'neka-*kidri' (headache) has uncertain diacritics.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain explicitly 'word or phrase' — the penultimate prominence may be phrase-level (utterance-penult) rather than strictly lexical word stress; statement is second-hand (Tucker & Bryan summarising Larochette 1958) and was read only through search snippets, not a held scan. Demolin's first-hand 1991 phonology sketch (held) describes tone and syllable structure but says nothing about stress. Alternative coding: tone language with a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's stress remark is attributed to 'MANGBETU' specifically (Larochette's Mangbetu proper = Glottolog Nuclear Mangbetu nucl1420), as distinct from 'MANGBETU-MEJE' used elsewhere in their chapter; Larochette 1958 and Vekens 1928 also cover Medje/Meje (meje1239) and Makere (make1250), all dialects of mang1394. Demolin 1991/1992 describe Mangbetu proper (nord-est Zaïre, Uele). Hartell 1993 and McKee's SIL work concern the Meje dialect.
